How Game Studios Should Allocate AI Budgets
0
How Top Studios Should Allocate Their AI Budgets
AI
Business
Oct 12
Written By
Michail Katkoff
Where game studios should spend their AI money, why the real bill runs about 30% over plan, and what that means for junior hires. By
Michail Katkoff
, based on his work with studios around the world.
Founders and execs keep asking me the same questions: how much are other studios spending on AI, and most importantly, on what? After working with studios around the world (and
counting the real cost of studio engineering
more than once), I’ve concluded the dollar figure matters far less than the allocation. And the honest answer adds up to more than 100%. Let me walk you through.
Start with the gap.
McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI
surveyed 1,719 people in 97 countries. 80% say AI has made them personally more productive. Only 37% say it has contributed to their company’s EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes), essentially unchanged from a year ago. The high performers are companies attributing at least 5% of EBIT to AI. In other words,
Individuals got faster, but the companies didn’t get richer.
Gaming shows the same split. In
Unity’s 2026 report
, just 5% of developers said they don’t use AI at all. Yet
GDC’s 2026 survey
found only 36% of developers personally use AI tools, and 52% say generative AI has hurt the industry, up from 30% a year earlier.
Studios buy the tools to be used by their people, who don’t trust them.
That gap is where studios are burning their AI budgets.
Most studios I see allocate the inverse of what works: the bulk of the budget goes into tool licenses spread across the org, a slice into a vague “innovation” function, and nothing into the boring work of rewiring how things get done. Last year’s McKinsey edition found that
fundamental workflow redesign had the strongest correlation with EBIT impact
of any attribute tested. Yet only a fifth of companies had done it.
You are not buying tools. You are buying a different way of working. The tools are the cheapest part of that purchase.
One more thing changed this year: AI stopped being priced like software. GitHub moved Copilot to usage-based billing in June. Agentic coding tools bill by the token.
Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in just four months
and now caps agentic coding spend at $1,500 per engineer per month. Budget AI like cloud: metered, capped, with one owner who looks at it every week. This pricing change has a fundamental impact on budgeting.
Here is how I would allocate the budget at a mid-size mobile studio today, in order of likely return.
For a $1M annual budget at a mid-size mobile studio:
UA creative pipeline (25%): tools plus the people who run them
Code assistance (25%): seats plus capped token spend
Text, localization and voice (10%): tools plus human QA on every locale
Art and asset production (10%): tools plus the person who stays current
Change management (30%): implementation lead, org-wide training, selected consultants, roadmap time for workflow redesign
1. UA creative pipeline (25%)
This is the most direct P&L line in the stack, and it isn’t close. Playables reached 13.3% of mobile gaming ad impressions in 2026, nearly doubling year over year according to
Sensor Tower
. The top studios now run some 100 playable concepts a month. The volume math has changed for good.
The reason is structural. Meta’s Andromeda and AppLovin’s Axon reward creative diversity at volume over clever targeting. The machine finds the audience pocket no human would have hypothesized. (More on that in
The UA System the Platforms Can’t Build for You
and our earlier look at
rethinking creative production with AI
.) The only thing the human controls is how many distinct shots on goal it gets.
The tools I’d look at:
Sett
to build the full agentic loop of ideation, generation, testing, and signal feedback.
Segwise
for creative intelligence, and the only platform I know of that tags playables at the interaction level.
Higgsfield
and
Layer
for brand-trained static and video at batch scale.
Playablemaker
for hand-built playables when a generated one won’t cut it.
If I had a live game and could fund only one AI initiative, this is where the money goes.
2. Code assistance (25%)
Engineers who tried Claude Code early on and hated it should look again. The models are meaningfully better, and they will be meaningfully better again in six months. Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel’s other top maintainer,
recently said AI-generated bug reports “aren’t slop anymore”
, and an experimental review system called Sashiko is catching real issues before they reach human reviewers. If the kernel takes this seriously, your live ops codebase has no excuse.
Be careful with productivity claims, mine included. METR’s 2025 study found experienced
developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster.
Its February 2026 update says developers are likely sped up now, but it can’t say by how much, because 30 to 50% of invited developers refused to work without AI. That refusal is a data point in itself.
The coding stack I’d recommend:
Cursor
and
GitHub Copilot
for daily IDE work.
Claude Code
and OpenAI’s
Codex
for agentic refactors and migrations.
Greptile
or
CodeRabbit
to catch issues before a human reviewer sees them.
This bucket gets 25%, up from what I’d have said six months ago, because the cost moved from seats to tokens. A heavy agentic user can run $1,000 to $2,000 a month. Cap it per head, review the top spenders monthly, and never put token counts on a leaderboard. Uber did, and the tokens became the KPI.
3. Text, localization, and voice (10%)
Localization, narrative, marketing copy, store descriptions, support macros, patch notes. This is the lowest-risk, highest-velocity category in the stack, and most studios still pay vendors to mark up frontier-model output and return it.
